answer.evidence: Three red seats in a row. The tall backrests (rows 5-18) are face-on vertical panels with horizontal stripes and a 2-row highlight at the top (rows 5-6), which is a rim. A dark line at row 17 separates the backrests from the seat. Below it, the seat cushion is a lighter band (L~120, rows 19-21) that ends in a front edge at row 21. Rows 22-24 are darker (L~66), a front face of 3 rows, and the legs and base in rows 25-28 add more. The seat top is 3 rows, which is thin but present, and the backrest is shown only as a vertical face.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate's 12 distinct colours are well below the 38-40 of the stall and well, and only on par with the hedge (11) and the smaller bench and lamp (14). Per-tile median is 11, comparable to the hedge (10), and flat-fill coverage is 0%, so density is not a problem on the numbers. Structurally, though, the red seats read as about 3 lightness steps (a light highlight on the cushion, a mid red, a dark red) plus a gold leg or base, against 5-6 steps on the references' main materials. The outline is a uniform near-black line around each seat. 100% of the dark edge pixels are neutral, versus 0% for the hedge and about 1% for the stall, which use tinted dark tones. This is the sticker look the standard rules out. Each seat is also a near-identical repeat with little per-seat texture or grain. The piece is clean and readable but shallower than the Beodeul material ramps, and the neutral outline is the deciding weakness.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is three red seats with gold legs. The measured facts back this up: 100% of dark edge pixels are near-neutral, so the outline is a uniform near-black line around every shape, the sticker look. The references mostly lean toward tinted outlines (hedge 0%, stall 1%, well 33%, bench 44%). The candidate has only 12 distinct colours against 38-40 for the richer references (stall, well).
